utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. You are alone, I see, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Halimi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Djurdjic is continuing with his questions. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Halimi. Yesterday we left off with that map, and I would like the legal officer, if he would be so kind, as to call up the Defence Exhibit D00065.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've brought up the unmarked map. Is that the one you want?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The map that is shown here is without any markings. Is that the one you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that we had admitted yesterday the map that Mr. Halimi had marked with this number, 00065.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll bring up D65.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, I'd like to know how far is Lower Zabare from Upper Zabare?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are the two villages are very close to each other. They are adjacent to the extent that few people would be able to differentiate between the Upper and the Lower Zhabar. However, if we were to try to tell the difference, at the time of the war from the centre of one village to the other, it would be a distance of no more than 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the questions I'm asking you refer to 1999. If I ever want to ask about another time, I'll make that known. Now, Mr. Halimi, from Upper Zabare to this closest area of the central urban part, how far is it?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How far is Lower Zabare from the closest part of the urban part of Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two to 2.5 kilometres. No more. Just over 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how far is Lower Zabare from Tavnik?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 1.200 metres? One kilometre and 200 metres, no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now how far is from Lower Zabare to Sipolje?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's approximately the same distance to Tavnik. Just about 1.200 metres, no more. This is just a guess on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how far is Lower Zabare from the Kovaci settlement?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 2 kilometres. I don't think it's 2. Approximately 2, but a bit less, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And also distance from Lower Zabare to the water-supply organisation?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies, it's no more than 1.200 metres. However, there are two roads, and I spoke on them yesterday, and depending on which one you take the distance varies. To be able to reach the water-supply company, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Approximately's good enough.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road that I emphasised yesterday, which is from the Zhabar school to the Shipol school, the one that is vertical, and the other one that joins the Mitrovica-Peje road and all the way to the water-supply unit should be approximately 2.5 kilometres. However, the other road which we say it's the one that takes you to the timber-processing compound should be about 500 metres more, which in my guess is about just over 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That you, Mr. Halimi. Your father, Mahmut, what was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father's name was Bajram, and he worked at the timber-processing unit in Mitrovica. Then he retired due to ill-health.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many siblings did you have?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had three brothers -- I have three brothers. I have two now. One has already died. There's three of us now and two sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a family house in Donje Zabare, in Lower Zabare?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In 1999 when the war began, who lived in that house?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That house belongs to me, has belonged to me since 1998. At the time, there were refugees from the Drenica region living in my house. So that house is to be found in the Zhabar compound. I lived there. After the war, I went and established myself with my family there. However, the house I stayed at during the war was the house that belongs to my brother which is closer to the city stadium and the Ibar River.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how about your father's family house? Who lived there? That is, where did your father live?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father died in 1986. At the time, me and my eldest brother, Hasan, lived together in Zhabar at the place where he still lives, which is the house adjacent to the Ibar River, which is on one extremity of Zhabar, closer to the city stadium. That was our extended family house. My brother still lives in that house whilst I went and had a house of my own built.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry about asking this. I had not seen that in the statement. Your mother was alive, though, at the beginning of the war, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother still lives. She's 84, nearing 85.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You are married, and you were married at the time when the war began. You had your wife and how many children?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my wife and four children. The same I had at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you were living, at that time, in an apartment in the northern part of Mitrovica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, it was a house which I bought towards the end of 1996, and I lived there until the 25th of March, 1999, which would make it a full ten years two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What were the ages of your children when the war began?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the eldest were the grown-ups, because of a gap between my second and third child, a gap of eight years, which means that my little daughter now is 17; she was of 9 at the time. Whilst my little son, who now is 15, was about 5 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how old were your first and the second child?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My eldest daughter, who is now married, was born in 1984, whereas my son is 23. He turned 23 on the 23rd of March, which means at the time he was about 13, whilst my daughter was 14 and a half, less than 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Halimi, in 1977 you got your law degree; and if I understood correctly, you found employment as a clerk on a trial period in the Municipal Court in Mitrovica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after this trial period that lasted one year, you were elected judge of the Municipal Court in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And tell me, under what law were you elected judge of the Municipal Court after just the trial period? After one year's apprenticeship?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] page on the law applicable at the time on the selection of judges, which was a prerogative of the Kosova Assembly. It was called the Law on the Appointment of Officials given that judges were part of the official structure of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Haven't judges always been part of the official structure?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were the ones who enjoyed official functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you claim here that an apprentice lawyer, having passed the bar exam, can legally be elected judge?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. You have to pass the exam to the bar, which applied across Yugoslavia at the time; and after completing this exam, every lawyer was entitled to apply to become a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about technical collaborator, independent assistant, research assistant? How many years does one have to work in these positions to gain experience?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lawyers who had gone through a period of apprenticeship at a court of law had a minimum period of one year to meet, whilst others who worked elsewhere, like at the municipality and so on, had a period of two years to complete of this kind of apprenticeship before they were able to sit the bar examination. Which means that they were entitled to apply for the position of a judge or a barrister, or, put otherwise, they would have the whole array of legal instruments at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halimi. You're now telling me about the requirements for taking the bar exam, and you are telling me that those who work in state agencies are eligible after one year and outside the state agencies it's two years. Now, I'm asking you in a court of law the technical assistant, independent assistant, and research assistant, who must already have passed the bar exam, also need to have a certain number of years of experience, but let's leave that aside. You left to do your military service in 1983, and in Bileca you attended the school for reserve officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started my military service in October 1980, and I spent it at the school for reserve officers at Bileca until the 31st of March -- or, rather, the 1st of April, 1981. Afterwards, I went to Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what rank did you get when you moved to the reserve force, having done your military service?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of my school years at Bileca -- I don't even know the term in Albanian, but I have to say it in Serbian. It was called the rank of Vodnik, which is a lower rank than the platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, would you listen to the questions that I'm asking you? I said when you had completed your military service - that's what I asked you - and when you moved to join the reserve force, what rank did you obtain at the time in the reserve force since you were attending the officers' school? You attended the officers' school while you were doing your military service.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of military manoeuvres of 1987, I was given the rank of captain of the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1992 you were elected judge of the Municipal Court in Sremska Mitrovica. You were appointed the judge there. Now, tell me, how long did you remain in that position as a judge of the Municipal Court?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see here in the transcript that the year recorded is 1992. Do you mean 1992 or 1982?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I meant 1982.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around May of 1982 I became a judge of the District Court of Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Like everyone else who was part of the ranks of officialdom, you wouldn't be able to join the service without joining the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, please, when did you cease to perform your functions as the -- as a judge of the District Court in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I terminated my work as a judge at the Municipal Court of Mitrovica at the end of 1985; and on January the 1st, 1986, I opened my private lawyer's office, a function which I continue to exercise today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to dwell too long on that period when you ceased to be a judge. I looked at your statement of the 31st of January, 2000. No, it wasn't 2000. 2001. It was the 24th of August, 2001. I looked at the official English version, and in that statement it says that you retired, that you retired. Now, what was the reason for that? Why did you leave your position as judge?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess it might be wrong, because I have the version in Albanian, and it does not mention anywhere that I ever retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'll read that part out to you, the English version. And it's signed, and this is what it says: "[In English] In the beginning of 1982, I became a judge in the District Court in Mitrovica. After my having my application approved for retirement, I eventually finished my careers as judge." [Interpretation] Mr. Halimi, this is a statement that you yourself signed. I won't go into the whole of the statement of what was noted at the end by the translator, interpreter, and your approval.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, Your Honours, I would like to clarify here. It is a fact that, with the applicable law at the time, the Assembly of Kosova would not issue an approval to abandon your post as a judge. I did make such an application to withdraw from the faction, but I was not approved of it; so according to law, I had to wait for six months for my mandate as a District Court judge to stop. So after this six-month period, I did abandon my post as a judge. I was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, we're talking about two different situations here. One is a situation where you tender a request to be relieved of your duties. That's one thing. At your own initiative and the Assembly has to decide upon that. And quite a different situation is when you retired, and you said that you had indeed retired. So these are two different bases for ceasing to work as a judge. Can you explain to us how it was possible that you said that you had retire, and you signed this statement of yours, which was the first statement you, in fact, gave to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement was read back to me in Albanian, and to my recollection, not in my statement to the investigators of the OTP and not even during my testimony here in the Milosevic trial and in the Milutinovic et al trial, this part was not mentioned; and as far as I know, I did clarify that it is true that I filed a request. This request was denied. And after six months, according to the law, my post as a judge no longer existed. It ceased to exist, and from that date I opened my private office and worked as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, I read out your statement, the statement you yourself signed, and it was written in English, and I'm now going to show you the certification by the translator of that same statement of the 1st of September, 2001. "Mahmut Halimi," it says, "told me that he speaks and understands the Albanian language, and the aforementioned statement I have translated from the English into Albanian in the presence of Mahmut Halimi, and it corresponds to the original, and judging -- and to all intents and purposes he understood the statement and the translation of it, and he confirmed that to the best of his recollections the facts set out in the statement are truthful as I have translated them and read back to him, and he asserts that by signing the statement."

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand English. I read the translation in Albanian, and I had no remarks as far as the Albanian translation is concerned. It is possible that an omission was made, or a mistake, not a deliberate mistake, on the part of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halimi. Let's move on. But while we're on the subject of mistakes, you said yesterday that in the transcript in the Milutinovic trial there was some mistakes made. How do you think those mistakes came about in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not an easy job for the interpreters, and such mistakes are possible. They can occur. However, from the context, you can easily tell that this is a mistake. As you saw yesterday, I reacted immediately when I saw my name on the transcript recorded as "Halilovic." I happened to notice that mistake, but as I said, mistakes can occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what you want to say is that everything is relative. Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the map is already an exhibit, D65, I believe; so I don't think it needs a number as the court officer has just told me. The only thing is that this witness has spoken about distances and kilometres, and they haven't been introduced onto this map. So, Your Honours, am I right in saying that this map does not need a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It has one already. It's Exhibit D65.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you became a lawyer and took up practice as a lawyer, did you specialise in any particular area of the law?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, as you may be well aware, at the time we belonged to the Yugoslav system there was no specialising in any particular area of the law. Everyone on his or her free will would orient himself or herself in what he or she wanted. Maybe I'm amongst the only lawyer in Kosova that deals with criminal cases, with criminal law mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So I can conclude that you're a specialist in criminal law. You decided to specialise in that area, and of course the state couldn't tell any of its lawyers or of the lawyers which area they would specialise in in their work. Am I right in saying that? It was your own choice?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you as a lawyer acted independently. You weren't a state official. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had my private office as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't understand you very well yesterday when you said that you were one of the first fighters against the judicial system that was in existence. Could you give me a time-frame? What period of time did you mean, and what did you mean when you said that?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say a fighter but a fierce opponent of the Milosevic regime, of the discriminatory nature, especially from 1990 onwards until the NATO air campaign began.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you give us some more facts, not just descriptions and qualifications, but the facts?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will illustrate it with a case that I well remember. The dates are between 31st of December, 1990, and especially 1st of January, 1991. That night, late at night, police forces surrounded our now legendary commander, Adem Jashari. He and his comrades succeeded in escaping from this encirclement by the Serb forces. On the following day, in the early morning hours, before 7.00, the police undertook measures against the inhabitants of Prekaz e Ulet village to retaliate and maltreated and beat about 27 or 29 citizens. I remember that day very well. It was a clear January day. It was very cold. We engaged ourselves for two and a half months. I personally engaged myself for two and a half months to defend five members of the extended family from the -- this village and presented this case and the difficult situation in general to the representatives of different organisations that were present at Kosova at the time. I familiarised them with this horror that the inhabitants of Prekaz and its outskirts had to suffer on this January day and also informed the media in Kosova and abroad. Of course the regime, at the time, didn't like this activity, was against this kind of activity, so lawyers, citizens, and everyone was, in a way, queuing to be interrogated in front of police stations of the Milosevic regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't understand you very well in the way that it was interpreted to me, but tell us, why are Mr. Jashari and the members of his group legend, or why did the legendary Mr. Jashari and his group flee from the police?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wanted by the police because of his public activities relating to the Kosova issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these activities that you mentioned, did they involve the use of fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, no. Perhaps only the sparks, because in lack of peaceful solution to the Kosova problem, it was expected that the Kosovan people will try and fight for their rights by resorting to arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems to me that you forgot that at that time in Sipolje, the legendary Mr. Jashari, with his group, killed a number of policemen?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't forget that. In 1991 and in 1992, there were no policemen killed in Shipol. Later on, yes. We have 1996, 1997, 1998 when policemen were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And was it whom you defended after the 1st of January, 1991? Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Prekaz e Ulet is mainly inhabited by members of Jashari family. There are also members of Lushtaku family, but most of the village is Jashari. I represented five persons, all of them Jashari -- Jasharis, they were not brothers or cousins of Adem Jashari. They were distantly related.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, you've been talking a lot, but you're not answering my question. What acts were they accused of having committed, and what acts did you defend them against?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the office of the prosecutor at the District Court in Mitrovica charged them with crimes of counter-revolutionary activity against the SFRY. They were kept in detention for three months. The penal criminal procedure stopped, was suspended, after three months because it was proved that they had nothing to do with the counter-revolutionary activity they were charged with at the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, from what you've just said, the judiciary functioned very well during Milosevic's time.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During his first years in power, the real nature of his regime was visible to all; and I think I managed to convey this through my own personal commitment and through soliciting the help of NGOs involved in human rights defences at the time, including Human Rights Watch, an organisation with which I had excellent contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Halimi, the police filed a report with the prosecutor's office instigated proceedings. The court established there is no basis for further prosecution, stopped the process, and acquitted these people. Does that mean that the judiciary were independent in their work?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did function somewhat. In fact, what was proven in -- through that process is that those five were part of the expeditionary nature of the police forces at the time, even the three months during which they were kept in detention, in fact were aimed at increasing repression with a view to hiding the repressive nature of the activities that the police themselves had undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halimi. You're not really being responsive, but let's move on. In your statement of 24 August 2001, you state: "I had to find all sorts of different ways to maintain good relations with the Serb authorities in Kosovska Mitrovica. I always had to act in the best interests of my clients. The hardest moments of my career were when I realised that everything is uncertain and unreliable but money. Unfortunately, those moments were frequent. It was awful for me to go back to my clients and tell them that they have to pay because Serbian justice exists only if one is ready to pay." Can you explain this part of your statement to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have considered myself the most fortunate of all if this had never occurred. However, this was part and parcel of a totalitarian country, of a criminal regime like the one that Milosevic led. I tried to explain yesterday the obvious instance where a judge at the District Court of Mitrovica had to take a petrol can, to take it to lawyers' offices - and we're talking here about lawyers who were involved in the same process - and I'm not -- talking here about money and corruption. It was a corrupt system, and I think the nature of this corruption, at the end of the day, worked badly against the Serbian people in Kosova and particularly in Serbia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but to begin with, I did not understand the bit where the judge was taking petrol canister to offices of lawyers in the same court. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's simple. You have an empty petrol can and you take it to the lawyer's office to have it filled with petrol. I.e., lawyers, solicitors, had to go and buy the petrol in about 20 minutes, 40 minutes, an hour's time. He returned and took the full petrol can to fill up his car or probably to sell it. There were quite a few solicitors in Mitrovica who experienced this kind of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that only through bribes you paid on behalf of your clients could you serve their interests. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the majority of cases, yes. I mentioned yesterday even at the municipal level, if citizens were to go to seek to have a birth certificate, which is an inherent right, a citizen was to pay an additional 10 Deutschmarks in order to obtain it, and this is in addition to the legal fees applicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halimi. We'll come back to that later, but I asked you for payoff -- asked you about payoffs in Serbian legal proceedings to get justice. You said that bribes were necessary to achieve that. Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need a minimum five hours to be able to explain this at some length, and I said this during my previous testimony as well. But from the municipal level, from the -- the flimsiest of offences and up to the Supreme Court of Serbia, all these echelons were heavily involved in taking bribes to be able to bring to a satisfactory resolution cases in which Albanians were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halimi. You understand perfectly well as a man who is a professional in criminal law that bribery is a double criminal act, a two-pronged criminal act. Is it clear to you that you were also responsible for a criminal act in making bribes, offering bribes on behalf of your clients?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot be held accountable of -- of criminal offences in a criminal system, within a criminal system, within a totalitarian system like the one that Milosevic led. You can not pretend to act normally. So from that point of view I would not consider it a criminal offence. And we are talking here about situations of extreme necessity, and you know that other considerations apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand you correctly that you believed that the situation justifies you in everything you did?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milosevic himself had legitimised this kind of activity at the time. He used to bring judges from all over Serbia to work in Municipal Courts inside Kosova. The excuse given was that this was a patriotic duty. In fact, the only duty that they had was to loot as much as they could. None of them were there to apply the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you were an active player in that system, offering bribes to judges; correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't describe myself as a key person. However, depending on circumstances and the explicit interest of both parties, as well as the duty one has to give the best in the defence of one's client, the ultimate resort or choice was to bribe the judges and prosecutors of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will never agree with your methods of work, and I don't think we can follow the principle that means justify everything, that any method is allowed in the representation of our clients. But tell me, Mr. Halimi, who was the president of the Supreme Court of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You do know that at that time the Supreme Court of Kosova had been suspended. It was only the Supreme Court of Serbia that was in operation. We are talking about 1990, the time when Kosova's autonomy was revoked. All its competent bodies were dissolved, including the Supreme Court of Kosova. So the authorities of -- the authority exercised until then by the Supreme Court of Kosova was passed on to the Supreme Court of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, by the constitution of Serbia of 1991, or 1992, I'm not sure, the unified judiciary -- judicial system was established for the first time headed by the Supreme Court of Serbia. Until that time, autonomous provinces had their own Supreme Courts. I'm asking you: Prior to the adoption of that constitution, who was the president of the Supreme Court of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, dear colleague, first of all, I -- I'm -- I'm not the only one who is a witness of the situation applying at that time. My honourable colleague as well. And we know that in March 1999, the constitution of Serbia, what we call the bloody constitution of Serbia, was approved. It was exactly the same day when they were toasting this approval whilst in Kosova a lot of blood was being shed. Let me refresh the memory of my own colleague. This did not happen in 1991. And from that moment onwards, it did not -- the Supreme Court did not exist. However, before 1989 there was an eminent lawyer called Riza Fazliu, who no longer lives. I think he was succeeded -- forgive me. Mr. Riza Fazliu was followed by someone else until 1989, but it ceased to exist in 1989. The only thing we had was a branch of the Supreme Court of Serbia based in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about Judge Pjeter Kolja? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. Thank you. Thank you. I forgot. Yes, Pjeter Kolja succeeded Riza Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I see from your statement that you are very familiar with Prizren. Is it true that Jakup Burmani was president of the District Court in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jakup not Burmani but Gurmani with a G. I don't think I ever met Gurmani. I've heard of him. I don't think I ever met him. However, I did hear of him. He was a judge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And was Judge Fadil Nushi, President of the Municipal Court?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I mean the period that you are talking about. Until 1991, before 1991.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know this person. However, let me explain the judicial system, a part of which I was myself. At the time, all judges and prosecutors, beginning from -- beginning at the end of 1989, were removed from their positions with full remuneration until the end of 1992. In 1992, however, an open competition was published on the nomination of judges even though this period of time from the end of 1989 to March 1992 was one in which Albanian -- very, very few Albanian judges worked, did any work. There was some prosecutors, but just very few judges. In 1992, however, an open competition was opened in which a negligible number of judges applied, because one of the conditions to apply was the explicit expression of loyalty to the state of Serbia. So from amongst the Albanians, there was a negligible number who would accept expressing an allegiance of loyalty to the State of Serbia. There were very few exceptions. There was one of the District Court of Prishtina. There was one or two in Mitrovica. There was one profession -- professional collaborator. This was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Halimi, up until the election of judges under the new constitution of Serbia, Albanians headed all the judicial organs in Kosovo and Metohija, and Skender Morine was the District Prosecutor in Kosovo until 1991 in Prizren. Jakup Gurmani was the President of the District Court. Fadil Nushi was President of the Municipal Court, and another Albanian was his predecessor as president of the District Court. Are you going to tell me after that there were no Albanians in the judicial system of Kosovo and Metohija who were brave enough to oppose all pressures and apply for positions of judges in open competition?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that I was one of those -- those who went to my colleagues and told them to not accept the apparatus of this regime, the nature of which was visible to us all, and I did help them, even materially speaking. I gave them money.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halimi. I forgot you called them collaborators a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were. Some of them even worse than collaborators, because they turned against their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you participate in the organisation of elections for the president of the Republic of Kosovo, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because at the time, I led the chapter of the Albanian Christian Democrat Party in Mitrovica. So, yes, I did take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also took part in the elections into the Assembly of Kosovo in 1991, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the elections to the Assembly and the referendum held on or around July the 2nd, and with which Kosova was declared a republic, a state with all the attributes of statehood, equal to the other constituent parts of the -- Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you participant in the adoption of the Kacanik constitution?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not there, no. Because those who participated were the delegates who had the vote of the people, our vote. They were the ones who gathered at Kacanik to endorse the contusion of the Republic of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And these enactments that we discussed and these processes we discussed, would you call that legal?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: History corroborated that. You do know that Kosova is now an independent country. More than 56 countries have recognised it. It was a reasonable course of events which ought to have been pursued, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to get involved in politics in the courtroom, and I'm not asking these questions for that purpose. I'm talking about 1991. And I'm saying that in a sovereign state, taking steps, the kind that you described, the state is then duty-bound to take all legal steps against those who jeopardised the order of the state, the constitutional order, and the legal order of that state. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we should deal here in science and not politics, and in order to become a scientist, one has to become impartial. If we are to deal in politics, you have your own viewpoint, and I have mine; and my viewpoint on the matter is that I was right and my people were right and they had to resort to all forms of repression on the part of the Milosevic regime because Albanians historically considered themselves to be a colony and the Serbian regime as a repressive one. I think I should not go into history, because history will tell you that Kosova has always been overwhelmingly inhabited by Albanians. And from the Second World War onwards, before the First World War, before the war of 1912, and so on, it had its own distinctive attributes; but this would take a long time to be able to explain this properly. It would take a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You are very loquacious in your answers, but let me make this question very simple. Just imagine, how would the government of the Republic of Germany react if Bavaria did what you did in Kosovo in 1991? What measures would the state of the Republic of Germany take?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should we not cite Southern Africa here? Why should we cite Germany? You know that Bavaria and all the other constituent elements of Germany have always been part and parcel of the same entity and having the same language and so on and so forth. Why then just cite here apartheid in Southern Africa which is very, very similar to the situation that applied in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, we've come to the time when we must have the first break. Could I point out that we have listened with complete patience for an hour and a half, and in that time you have not asked questions about the events of -- that are relevant to the indictment; and you are, at the moment, pursuing questions dealing with the subject of political philosophy, which is not going to assist this Chamber to determine the question of the guilt or innocence of your client. It's a matter of deep debate about which clearly different views can be taken, but this Chamber in this trial is not going to be in a position to say one side is right or one side is wrong. That is not a matter we must deal with. We have an indictment alleging offences, and they are the matters to which we must direct our attention, so that we would be very grateful when we return after the break if you were able to direct any questions you have dealing with the issues that will concern us in the trial. Thank you. We must now have the first break, and we will resume again at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, in your statement from 2001, you said that you worked with the Kosovo Verification Mission. Can you tell me what your involvement with that was and what your task was? But please just briefly. Stick to the facts, please.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that this happened on the 5th of October, 1998, when the international community diplomatic mission to Kosovo was deployed. It followed the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement, if you recall that. I'd been invited as a representative of the Mitrovica region, and I recall this -- I recall this with some clarity, because I had to take an oath, an oath to say that I should serve with the mission, to pass on information depending on the itinerary and the other plans that they had as part and parcel of their remit there. This is the KDOM mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And could you tell me what reports you sent, and were you a member of the mission? What was your status? Were you an associate or what?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though the primary goal of that mission was to obtain a stable situation in Kosova, that Serbian units refrain from violence and so on, I as a collaborator of this mission was duty-bound to convey to the mission in what way was the agreement being implemented on the ground, i.e., vis-a-vis, the commitment made by Mr. Milosevic in front of Mr. Holbrooke, namely the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you some short questions, and please give me yes or no answers. Were you paid by KDOM?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They made an offer which I turned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign a contract with them?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, with the exception of the oath which I had to sign in their presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What reports and how often did you send them out?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minimum of two or three reports a week, sometimes written, sometimes imparted orally, all of them aimed at giving a chronological account of what was happening in the region of Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you report on the activities of the KLA? I mean, did you report to KDOM about that?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made -- I even made possible direct contacts with them. So I enabled contacts between them and representatives of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me who you established contact with? Who in the KLA, and who in KDOM?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that the region of Mitrovica belonged to two of the military zones of the KLA, one being the zone of Drenica, the other one of Shala, I advised them to establish contacts; and to this end, I resorted to the links that I myself had with the representatives of the KLA. They did not hold their meetings in my presence, i.e., I was not present there. I think their main interest was that I be not seen in their presence by the Serbs whilst they went to meet KLA members, and that explains why they had their contacts separately. I don't know who they met at that stage, but certainly it must have been the representatives of that military force at the time. Or, rather, military representatives of the mission at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you give me the names of the KLA members that you linked up with KDOM?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- it was liaison -- a liaison type of role between me, foot soldiers, and commanding structures of the KLA. Let me try to recall two or three people I had most contacts with, meaning that we enjoyed a maximum amount of trust. Dzevad Valci [phoen], Nedzad Curbrali [phoen], Ismet Hadza [phoen] in particular. These are people who I trusted not to spy on me at the Serbian police, and what they did is convey information as to the venue where they would wait for the representatives of the mission, which is what they did. They waited for them, and they arrived at an agreement as to where to meet. Let me reiterate, though, that I was not present at one of those meetings. This was not part and parcel of my remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halimi. Now, could you tell me who it was from KDOM that you linked up to the persons you've just named? Could you give me the names of the KDOM people? Kosovo Verification Mission is what KDOM is short for -- or, rather, KFOR.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the KDOM representative for Mitrovica was someone from Finland called Teutikam [as interpreted]. I think he a was high-ranking diplomatic representative. To be frank with you, I never involved myself in trying to find out their professional background, but he lead the mission. He was the one I had most contacts with. There was another one from France. I can't remember his name. Another representative from Greece. Another one was German. It was four or five in general. However, most of my contacts were with Mr. Tikkanen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you know, did you inform anybody that the H -- that the KLA had taken control of territory from which the police and army of the Republic of Serbia had withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went and saw it with their own eyes. It is well known now that the KLA had control and -- over a part of the territory of Kosova in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, in your statement you mention, although I don't understand this very well, a group -- the kidnapping of some kind. Could you tell me first what period you're referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the end of 1998. In the first two months I, in the period running up to the NATO air-strikes, where specialised police units, one of which was -- had established itself at hotel number 3 at Zvecan and the other one at the military barracks in the centre of Mitrovica at the secondary school where the old barracks are located -- were located. During the Milosevic period, the Special Forces Unit of the MUP of Serbia was established within these barracks, and it is from here that they went hunting for Albanians, as it were, usually in the -- after 22.30, 23.00 in the evening. And so they kidnapped a number of people whose remains were only found two or three days later in various locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how do you come to know that, what you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this very well, because these infamous units undertook their activities at the same time. They left the barracks roughly at the same time, only to return there in the early hours of the morning. I myself have observed them from the first floor of a nearby building, of a building that's alongside the road that takes you to the barracks; and I remember that they used a white Land Rover car, which often had German registration plates. I assume it was an armoured car, but I'm not sure about it. It had dark windows. There were also three or four others in a Fica car, which is one of the models of the Zastava factory. It's only on the following day that one would learn that two, three, four Albanians were found dead, i.e., executed in different locations around Mitrovica. I used to observe them for days on end from a building near the secondary school, from the first floor of that building. It's about 25 metres from the entrance to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the basis of the fact that these vehicles went in and out, you made these conclusions. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is more than correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Halimi, you said that someone threatened you when the KLM [as interpreted] left Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or, rather, the Kosovo Verification Mission, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you explain to us what happened, but just briefly, please, when the KVM left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From early October and until 26th of November, 1998, the KDOM was operating there. It was followed by the OSCE, which mission continued until some days before the NATO air-strikes began. It is true that I received a threat on the 23rd of March in the evening. It was my son's birthday. My son's name is Ylber. And after these gun-shots were heard, if necessary I can describe this in details because I will never forget it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You established that that was Sinisa Lazic, you say. Now, tell us who Sinisa Lazic.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it is an employee at the municipality of Mitrovica, at the time someone who I knew very well and who I helped a lot before the NATO air-strikes, during the war. Because I didn't want to discriminate between ethnicities, I offered my assistance and help to Serbs and Albanians as well. A Serb had killed his uncle's son, and I represented the family of the deceased during these proceedings. This is the person in question. And this is how he wanted to repay for my assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I asked you was what he did, but you gave a very long answer about what I hadn't actually asked you. What function and post did he hold, if he had any?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he was an official at the municipality. He was a part of an inspectorate, but I'm not quite sure which inspectorate he worked with. Financial inspectorate or market inspectorate. I really don't remember which one he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you went to see him in the morning and that you said to him, "Remember this and tell everyone else who's like you that you come from the Carpathians, whereas I and my people have been living here for 2.000 years, and as of this day you are my greatest enemies"?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. I didn't say "you" in plural, but I said "you," in singular, "will be my greatest enemy from now on." If you say you in plural that implies the whole Serbian nation, and that's not what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: There must be a mistake again in the interpretation, Mr. Halimi, because everything that doesn't suit you seems to be an interpretation mistake, but let's move on. Am I right in saying that in 1998 you were warned of some threats?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were systematic threats, I would say, dating back from 1990. And I was proud of myself working on the fundamental issues concerning my people and being part of those who brought freedom to Kosova. There were continuous and systematic threats, but what touched me most was the threat coming from this person whom I knew very well and who I helped a lot. I don't know how you would feel if you were in my shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the 25th of March, someone threatened you again. 1999, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 25th of March, I was warned. I received a phone call, and I was informed that my life and the lives of my family members were threatened. The person who called me on at that day did not threaten me, but, rather, asked me to leave, fearing that something might happen to me what happened actually to Latif Berisha and Agim Hajrizi on the night between the 24th and 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I already explained yesterday. I took the luggage that was ready in the corridor, my children, my wife, put them in the car, and drove to the stadium, crossed the Ibar River, and went to Zhabar. I left my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, in Zabare, how did the KLA learn of the fact that you were in a house there?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't stay locked in a room in Zhabar. I would go out in the yard, communicate with hundreds and thousands of citizens who were gathered in that village. I was not hiding in a basement or cellar. I was there in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, my question was: How did the members of the KLA find out that you were in Lower Zabare, in the house? Can you tell me or not?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two- or three-member patrols of the KLA, patrols that would observe the situation in Zhabar because of this great influx of people in this village. I personally met them, greeted them in the street. They were not dressed in uniforms. They were in civilian clothes, but I knew them as members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And why did you have to leave Lower Zabare according to them?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the third day, as I've already explained it yesterday during my testimony and earlier, in Tamnik neighbourhood, which is kind of a neighbourhood of Mitrovica, there was a police attack. Some citizens were captured by the police, and they were specifically asked about me; and that's why that evening, on the third night, on the 28th of March, in the evening hours after 8.00 p.m., in order not to put the life and security of the refugees and other inhabitants of Zhabar at risk, I -- as it was in other cases when hundreds of people were massacred because of one person, I decided to leave my brother's house and go to Upper Zhabar. I went to the Grmova mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, did the members of the KLA who called on you in Zabare have weapons or not?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't see that. Maybe they had small weapons on them. I didn't ask them to show me their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said they were not armed in your statement. I just wanted to ask you, was there a KLA hospital as well in this village, Lower Zabare?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the house of my relative Ymer Idrizi. It was a make-shift clinic that treated the ill and the wounded KLA soldiers, soldiers that were wounded in different areas. The main person who looked after them was Dr. Bajram Rexhepi who is now the mayor of Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that uniformed and armed members of the KLA did not come to the village in order not to attract police forces into the village housing their hospital, the KLA hospital?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right then in thinking that the police found out the KLA hospital was there and that's why they entered your village a couple of days later?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The police had no knowledge of it. The police had a planned itinerary, a plan to carry out an ethnic cleansing of this village and to expel the population to Albania. The reason was not the existence of this clinic who treated civilians and wounded KLA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, the reason was not the KLA in the mountains where you went to, was it?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. The KLA soldiers, where I was in the mountains with my friends, were only looking after us, providing us with food. They had no means and capacities to defend us in case of an armed attack. There, too, two or three KLA soldiers would come to see us. The main roads were very near. There were Serb forces on all sides. There were artillery forces nearby. So it was not possible for them to confront these forces. They were not in position to defend us in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far away were you from those roads?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies from the place where I was at the time - I'm speaking about the period of time when I left my house and stayed there together with other intellectuals from Mitrovica - the distance between this place and the Adriatic highway that continues to Montenegro is not more than 300 or 350 metres, as the crow flies, as I said. Whereas the Peje-Mitrovica road, about 1 kilometre far. I can show it on the map if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later. Am I then right that the check-points for the search of persons moving along those roads were a way of discovering weapons and detecting KLA members mingling with the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They knew very well that there were no members of the KLA in the columns, in the convoy. Everybody would have joined the KLA had there been enough weapons. This is my opinion. But I guarantee you that not a single KLA member abandoned his weapon to join the convoy of civilians and abandon his tasks and duties received from the higher military structures. So this was not the reason of these -- the existence of these check-points. The police would carry out systematic looting of these abandoned villages. So this was their primary task not to check the civilians from the convoy but to loot them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how do you know all this that you told me about members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I come from that area, and I knew many KLA members; and I was familiar with the level of morale amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And all this that you are telling us about the convoys and the number of people is something you observed from the mountains while making your own conclusions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The things that I saw occurred between 14th, 15th, and 16th April, the 16th April being the date when I join the column. At around 12.30 a.m. on the 16 -- 17th of April - correction - I joined the column together with my relatives and acquaintances from Zhabar, Mitrovica, and the surrounding area. So this is the situation prevailing on these dates, 14th, 15th, and 16th of April, the situation that I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far away were you from the Kovaci neighbourhood at the time?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kovaci neighbourhood is quite far. You could only see the smoke coming out of the houses and the buildings. As the crow flies, that would be about 3 or 4 kilometres far. I'm speaking about the Kovaci neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in thinking that you were not an eye-witness to the incident where 26 Albanians were killed in Kovaci?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. I was not an eye-witness to this incident; but after the war, together with CCIU, I took part in the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you an eye-witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you see the school in Sipolje from the place you were?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already mentioned it yesterday that you cannot see the school building at Shipol from there, but you can see the road from Zhabar that stretches up to a location or a playground behind the school. That one you can see very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask D00065 to be called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you what is this area north of the Ibar River on this map?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Can you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Looking at the map, which area on this map is north of the Ibar River?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The northern part of Mitrovica is north of Ibar River, Suhadol, Fusharc, Vinarce, Vidimiric, Caber, which belongs to the Zubin Potok municipality. These are the villages that are north of Ibar River.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far away were you when you were in Upper Zhabar from that area north of Ibar?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends. These villages are not too far from each other but not too close either. From Suhadol to the Vinarce which is the last, Vidimiric is on a hill-side. You can see half of it, half you can't. So if you were to take into account 200, 250 metres from the road, and near the road you can find Ibar. Then there's 200, 250 metres of fields. So I'd say it's about Vinarce, Bushac, the upper and the lower one, all of them are at a distance of about 700 metres from where I was, from where I did my observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand. From Upper Zabare, where you are in your house, to the village north of the Ibar River, there's 700 metres?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that in the map if you want to. Look at the Grmova mountain. It's at an altitude of 793 metres, and look at the Adriatic highway that takes you to Zubin Potok and Montenegro, and look at the Ibar River, or you can do the measurements yourself or call an expert in topography here, in mapmaking, to be able to do the measurements, and it is not more than 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vidimiric is about 1 kilometre away from Vinarce and Bushac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were able to see with your naked eye the people in those villages north of the Ibar River?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They looked very, very small, like ants, but you could see a massive influx. You could see that they were people fleeing their homes towards the Ibar River and converging on Zhabar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your brother's son a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a manner of speaking, we all were. Amongst them, the -- my brother's two sons. However, they were not soldiers in uniform, because there were no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What did you think about the fact that 30.000 people were sent off towards Srbica and Pec?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very familiar with my place of birth. I'm aware of the surface area, and that includes knowledge that I've obtained through my military experience. I would say that that number should be a very close approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but there have been witnesses here who also offer approximate figures that are much lower, but let's move on. You say Serb forces came into the village or the outskirts of the village and started shooting from automatic weapons. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to Upper Zhabar, yes, I witnessed -- I witnessed that myself. It was on the 16th of April, around 10.00. It could be just before or just after 10.00, where, as I stated before, the last car of the convoy was behind the school, i.e., of the convoy heading towards Peje. And as soon as the last car disappeared from view, i.e., ten minutes or so later, police forces came into the flat area of Zhabar e Eperme, Upper Zhabar, because Zhabar is on two plains. One is flat and the other one heads towards the hill a bit. So seen from the eastern point of view, I -- right in front of the place where the sun rises, I was able to observe the views. Just after 10.00 we heard shooting and we saw two or three, I think there were three houses -- where smoke was coming out of. There was gun shooting and then we saw inhabitants coming out of the flat part of Zhabar and heading towards the Adriatic highway. Some of them went towards Mitrovica. The others took a right and went towards that timber-processing plant, if I can call it a plant. It's a number of enterprises that do timber processing. And it's only afterwards that we understood that they had suffered very badly. They stayed there all night. Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but will you just tell me what happened with the hospital and the wounded?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is, and as I've explained it happened either on the 12th or 13th of March -- forgive me, no, April, like I say as I explained earlier in my testimony, from Suhadol there was a police intervention and they were focusing on Zhabar. This comprised armed units which were using the -- some sort of armoured car called Praga which I had not seen before even as a military -- even seen from my military experience. They started from Zhabar. My mother, at that stage, was 75 years old, and so in view of what happened, I decided to go to the Upper Zhabar. I think this occurred around the 13th of April, i.e., the time me and my family went to Upper Zhabar. So from the 13th of April onwards, I was not aware of what happened to the hospital and the wounded. They must certainly have left too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm waiting because the interpretation lags behind a little, and only when the witness finished the interpreter started to interpret. There is no other problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that those Serb forces then continued on towards Upper Zhabar?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain this chronologically so that the situation becomes entirely clear. After 10.00, i.e., at about 11.00, police forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- your statement. All we need is to clarify certain points in it. Or, rather, I need clarification. So everything you've said up until now is what we can read in your statement, but I would like some clarifications. And what I'm interested in is this: Whether the forces going from Donji, Lower Zhabar police ones and military ones continued on to Upper Zhabar.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it impossible to give a response if I'm not allowed to give a sequence of events of which I was an eye-witness. I was only at a distance of 50 metres from the police, the paramilitaries, and the army people; and that is the point in time when me and my family descended and saw them with my own eyes. They were on the left-hand side --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- interrupt you again, Witness. We have all that in your statement. What I asked you is this: The forces that passed through Lower Zabare, did they go to Upper Zabare and further on? That's all I'm interested in. Did they go up there or not?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces that were in upper -- in Lower Zhabar joined the forces that had been deployed throughout the Upper Zhabar, creating an uninterrupted supply of police, paramilitary, and military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was there a conflict between the KLA and the forces that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no clash whatsoever, with the exception of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Witness. What happened to the members of the KLA with whom you were when these other forces arrived?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that KLA members were with me all the time. I said that they did come from time to time to look after us. They had their own units deployed in Vaganica, Lubovac, and so on and so forth, engaged in their own military activities. I was not saying here that there were KLA members with us all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So what were these KLA activities? Tell us about them.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the place where I was staying. All that was offered to us was food and cigarettes. So they were trying to look after us even in those utterly difficult circumstances, whereas regarding military clashes, they were occurring, as you very well know, from Vaganica and other places. There was fierce clashing between Serbian police and army forces and the KLA troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And from the Vaganica area and direction, did the civilian population go from there?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained it, it happened on the 14th of April. They suffered the same fate, chased away by Serbian police and army forces. They did not leave of their own free will. They did not live their homes and come all the way to Zhabar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've just said that in Vaganjica there was a clash between the KLA and the Serb forces. And that armed combat took place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you ought to have some information about Vaganica, how big it is and what it is a party of. Where the civilian population of Vaganica was, it was almost joined up to the village of Shipol, whereas the other part of Vaganica which is separated by the Lushte river is the place where the military activities were occurring, which then continued in Pirc, Vinarce, Lubovec, and all the way to Prekaz.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what you want to say is that the civilians sat quietly in their part of Vaganica village while there was fighting across the river. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had nowhere else to go. In such circumstances, with this danger posed on them, they had to stay somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the time you were in the village, was there any bombing going on, NATO bombing of Mitrovica and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what parts of Mitrovica were bombed?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I personally saw was the military barracks at Svinjare. I think it was bombed on the 15th of April, if I remember correctly. It was hit three or four times. And following this, the mines exploded around the complex of military barracks there. I observed this from where I was. These were mines that were placed around the fence around the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the place you were at, you didn't see that a civilian -- any civilian facility was damaged. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, in Mitrovica there were no such cases. After the war, however, I heard that the -- a civilian facility next to the police station that had been hit by NATO was destroyed and a woman had died as a result of the building being bombed, the police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what you mean when you say "paramilitary formation"?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, a paramilitary formation would be an organised gang of people with experience from Bosnia and Croatia organised in such a way that they were placed under the command of the police and military structures. And as gangs, they took part in the looting, in the sexual assaults, and other forms of crimes. For example, Arkan's Tigers; the unit of Frenki Simatovic, although it was within the framework of MUP and you know that very well; and other organised units that in a way imitated the Arkan unit, which were situated at the police station in Mitrovica during 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how do you differentiate between the paramilitary formations and official formations or units?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were different in terms of uniforms, structure. They were smaller. They operated in smaller groups. And difference in terms of behaviour, a behaviour typical for them demonstrated in the wars in Bosnia and Croatia and repeated in the war in Kosovo. If you would like to hear more, I can illustrate what I said with an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how do you call the mobilised reserve force, and how do you differentiate between that force and these other formations and units?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were more like supporting units, I would say. An accessory. They wore old type of military uniforms, the olive-grey uniforms. As it is called in Serbian, SMB, from the time of Tito. This is what I saw in the location between the villages of Cubren and Vitak near the telephone cables that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were in a car with your family, in a column, when you set out towards Pec. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The last in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What documents did you have on you?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I had my ID, driver's licence, car registration document. I'm not sure whether my car registration document was seized by the police when they seized my car. This I don't know for sure. They seized my car, the car of my brother, and my brother's son-in-law as we came down from Zhabar. I had a Mercedes make car, 190 type. I'm sure I had my ID and my driver's licence on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I think that these cars -- as far as these cars are concerned, your brother went to fetch them, but they were not in working order and that he wasn't able to switch the engine on.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wouldn't be correct. If you read my statement carefully, it should say that my brother and his son-in-law, the following day, after hearing from some citizens that the police were selling the same cars that they had seized from citizens, they set out to get back the vehicles we had. When they went there, they couldn't find our cars. A policeman called Novica from Zubin Potok, who knew my brother, made it possible for him to go to the neighbourhood and choose a car. So it is not true that we left the cars because the engines wouldn't start. Our cars were taken by the police, the three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And which cars were you in when you were in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained this too. When we arrived at Shipol school and the lower part of the road, about 50 metres away from the fence of the school-yard, there there were different cars. My brother's son-in-law, who was a car mechanic, although he is an economist by profession, but he was taught in this business by his father, he managed to start the car and brought this Golf-make car to me.
