We were eight in the Golf, and then we towed a Moskowich that we found on the road, and we towed the Moskowich up to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that none of your documents were confiscated?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can you possibly be right when I already told you that they seized my car registration document when they seized my car? At the border, I handed over the other documents. I know that after we crossed the border my passport was found in the luggage with our clothes. My wife found it and told me that I had my passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But you had your car registration --

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Driver's licence. [In English] My driving licence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said that you weren't searched at the border crossing by the policeman.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the border crossing, at the facility there, they would shout, "To the right, to the right, and straight to Albania." Nobody would body-search us there; but as we were waiting in the column to cross the border, a policeman would come and ask for all personal documents, passports, IDs, driver's licence, car registration, borders, and they will tell us to leave or hand over these documents at the crossing. Otherwise, if they find documents on us, they would kill us. So the people were throwing away their personal documents out of fear, and you could tell that their aim was to deprive us of our identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, my question was: Am I right in saying that you were not searched at the border crossing by the police?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a different question. It is true that at the border crossing we were not searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you do not have any immediate personal knowledge as to who set your house on fire and in what way this was done in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out in the meantime, and I sent a message.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was that you weren't an eye-witness. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was told by others that my house was set on fire on the 3rd or 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you weren't a witness to how the mosque in Mitrovica was damaged?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you weren't an eye-witness of the killing of Jatif [as interpreted] Berisha?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, and this is in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You weren't an eye-witness to the killing of Jahim [as interpreted] Hajrizi either, were you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- right in saying --

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- Agim Hajrizi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: A correction to the name. Yes, I apologise if I mispronounced, but am I right in saying that during your journey to the border, you weren't looted?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I wasn't looted. I was lucky not to be looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to ask you one more thing, Mr. Halimi. You became a judge again. You took up your job as a judge after the war in 1999; right?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As of 1st of September, 1999, judge at the District Court in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And for how long were you a judge of the District Court in Mitrovica? Until when?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some 22 or 23 months. Sometime until April 2001. Until April 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And why did you cease being a judge?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the decision to apply for the post of a judge was made on the recommendation of my colleagues from the OSCE so that I could continue to contribute to the judicial system in Kosova after the war. However, I was in love with what I was doing, working as a lawyer; so for these 22 or 23 months, I think I did give a considerable contribution to the development of the judicial system in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that among other things you were the judge in -- in the trial of individuals who were accused of the killing of your friend Hajrizi?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mitrovica, known as a multi-ethnic city, we had almost every ethnic group of Europe as an inhabitant of Mitrovica. It is true that I was judge in that trial. I've perhaps explained it earlier. I was quite emotional about this young man. I could never understand why this hatred. Nenad Pavicevic and Agim Hajrizi lived very close. Only a wall separated their house. They grew up together. So why all this hatred?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So you believe there was no reason for accusal, and you were an objective judge, but I wanted to ask you something else. Do you think that a person who has offered a bribe to judges in his life, and done similar deeds, meets the moral requirements to perform as a judge?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left everything behind with the end of the war. The end of the war changed everything in Kosova. It changed the morale, as well what we once were forced to do that, now we were committed to do that. If Kosova was well established, and if someone else was prepared to take up that case, I wouldn't have been involved. However, the Trial Chamber asked for a copy from this judgement, and I wish that the Trial Chamber has a copy of that judgement and appreciate how fair that judgement was. We were impartial. A Swedish judge was member of that Trial Chamber. He was an excellent judge. He helped me a lot, not only in this case but in other cases that I tried at this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halimi, but I think that ethics do not change depending on the circumstances and that human values are the same in any period of time. You have no further questions. Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you, Your Honours, for your patience in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we must have that second break now, and we will resume again at 1.00 for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can indicate that I have no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, you will be pleased to learn that that concludes the questioning of you. We have the oral evidence that you've given to us and the transcript of your previous evidence. We wish to thank you for your assistance and for coming here yet again to give evidence. You are now, of course, free to go to your ordinary activities, and the court officer will show you out. So thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar, are you able to assist us with the programme for the rest of today? Is there another witness ready at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Your Honours, and it's Ms. Sadiku. Silvia D'Ascoli will be questioning her, and she's ready, she can appear after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will then resume at five minutes past 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I think Ms. D'Ascoli has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour. Before we start I can indicate that Ms. Sadiku's evidence relates to paragraph 72(f), 73, and 77 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Sadije Sadiku.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And when and where were you born, Ms. Sadiku?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: I was born on July the 1st, 1978, in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Where are you currently residing?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: I -- I live at Sabor e Eperme, or Upper Zhabar.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: -- employed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, on the 15 of August, 2006, did you provide a statement to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor events that you had experienced and witnessed in Mitrovica in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And have you recently had the opportunity to review your written statement?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that information contained in it is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the 65 ter number 02256, which is Ms. Sadiku's witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00502, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. And I should mention, Your Honours, that attached to the statement are the witness medical reports from Albania and Germany where Ms. Sadiku was hospitalised in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, did you also testify about the same events before this Tribunal in the Milutinovic et al case August 2006?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review the transcript of your testimony in the Milutinovic et al case?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And does the transcript accurately reflect your evidence, and would you testify to the same facts today?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the 65 ter number 05141 into evidence, please. It is the transcript of Ms. Sadiku's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00503, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now proceed to read a summary of this witness evidence. The witness is a Kosovo Albanian from the village of Zhabar in Mitrovica. She describes the forcible expulsion of Kosovo Albanians from Zhabar in mid-April 1999. On the 13th of April, 1999, the police began burning houses in Zhabar and expelling people from their houses. The following day, the witness and her family were told to leave by the police. They joined a column of people headed towards Albania. They marched for some days. A part of the convoy of refugees was then directed to the village of Zablace and was told by the police to stay there. The witness was in the group of people she remained in Zablace for three weeks at all time watched over by the police. On 6 May, 1999, in Zablace, the witness was hit in her back by a sniper. She was taken for basic medical assistance to the village of Zahac. When the Serb police expelled people also from Zahac, the refugees proceeded in a convoy towards Albania finally crossing the Albanian border on the 12th of May, 1999. And the witness was in that convoy. In Albania, the witness was taken to the hospital in Tirana where she received the medical assistance and had the first surgery. She was later transferred to Germany for further medical assistance. The witness is paralysed as a result of those injuries. And this is the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, I will now move to your statement and ask you some questions to clarify some events. Can you tell us where were you living in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Until April the 13th, we lived in the village of Zhabar. On the 13th of April, Serbian forces starting setting fire to the houses in that village forcing us to go to the mountains. On the 13th of April, we spent the night up in the mountains in the cold and the rain. There were too many of us, and there was absolutely nowhere to stay, to seek shelter. We returned on the following day because a lot of rain had fallen. We'd had nothing to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sorry, may I stop you there. How far is the village of Zhabar from Mitrovica town approximately?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And you just mentioned that there were people who fled with you to the forest on the night of the 13th of April. Can you tell us what their ethnicity was and why they also had left their villages?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: We were all Albanians. We were forced out of our homes. The only place where we could find some shelter was at Zhabare e Eperme; that is my village. And I'm referring to the period up to the 13th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And before I interrupted you, you were about to describe what happened the following day on the 14th of April when you returned to your house. Can you please describe what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Okay. We returned on the 14th of April to have a change of clothes because we'd been soaked, as a result of the rain. As soon as we changed and we started preparing something to eat, Serbian forces arrived in the village and forced us out again through the use of force.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And in paragraph 14 of your statement you say that the police at gunpoint threatened you and told you to leave the house immediately. Did they give you an explanation for that? Did they tell you why you had to leave?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: They came into the house. They -- at gunpoint they told us to leave the home within five minutes, otherwise they'd kill us all.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 you mention that while marching in the column of refugees that you joined, you passed by a number of check-points. Can you tell us who was manning those check-points?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes. There were Serbian police and soldiers as well in the majority of the places we went through.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could you describe the police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes. It was blue and black.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, I will now show you a photo-board.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I please have on the screen 65 ter number 02375. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, is there any --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yeah, that's fine, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, is there any among these pictures which represents the uniforms, the colours of uniforms that you saw in April 1999? The one that you just described now. Could you indicate that to us?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Maybe you could place a cross close to the picture that you recognise, if you can.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: It's that one there.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And this resembles which -- which uniforms or which forces that you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: It belongs to the police forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit as marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00504, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I should mention that the same photo-board is one of the attachments to the witness statement, but there it is only a photocopy and not in colour. Therefore, it is not visible exactly the type of uniforms that the witness marked, so maybe with this colour copy it is a better visual aid for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, now let's go back to your statement. There you mention in paragraphs 18 and 19 that you kept walking in the column of people for two or three days without any rest and that you were all very exhausted and in bad condition and that the police told you to continue marching. I was wondering, can you please tell us the direction you took when you left your village, Zhabar, on that morning of the 14th of April?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: In the morning of the 14th of April we were told to go to the main road. As soon as we arrived, some other policemen who were stationed in the village told us to go to some sort of a lumberyard to join up with the other people already gathered there.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the locations where you were heading to or where you arrived or passed by?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: This place is at Zhabar Ulet. Lower Zhabar. It is in between Zhabar Ulet or lower Zhabar and Shipol.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: So they brought us together at this location, and on the following day they told us to go to Tirana. They said everybody had to leave Kosovo and go to Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a map. Probably that can assist us to identify the places you went through.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I please have on the screen the 65 ter number 00039. Thanks. If we can enlarge, zoom a bit on the top part of the map. Maybe a bit more. Yeah, that's enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Are you able to see properly, Ms. Sadiku?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I was wondering whether you can recognise or identify your village, Zhabar, on this map.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could you please encircle it and maybe place a number 1 close to it.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you also see the following places where you went to afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you please specify them, name them?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: From Zhabar we went to Shipol, and from Shipol to Lushte.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could you please encircle the village of Shipol. Put a number 2 close to it?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please do the same with Lushte. Mark on it with the number 3 please?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember where you went to after Lushte?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: After Lushte we went to Kline e Eperme, or upper Kline.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you see this village on the map, Ms. Sadiku?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: I can see it. However, in this map of yours all that's written is "Middle Kline." However, it is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Because you mentioned Kline e Eperme, right, which is Upper Klina.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Did you also pass by Klina -- Middle Klina, Kline e Mesme, I think?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could you please encircle this village and put a number 4 close to it.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this exhibit as marked by the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00505, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. I see my learned friend on his feet, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have no objection. I just want to say that on the map we can see the upper Drina River, and the witness can right below Lower Klina locate Upper Klina and she can mark.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. She mentioned that she passed through Kline e Eperme and then from -- also Kline e Mesme. So I think that's enough. She couldn't locate it on the map, so that's fine, but thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, after passing through Klina, and you passed through the Skenderaj municipality, you then proceeded towards Peje, and in paragraph 23 to 24 of your statement you say that the police at some point ordered you to stay -- to go and to stay in the village of Zablace. The village was deserted and then you remained there for about three weeks. Ms. Sadiku, can you please describe to us what happened to you on the 6th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: We were forced by the police to go to the village of Zablace, not Zahac, where we spent three weeks. There was nothing to eat at the end of the three-week period because the village had been shelled. The villagers had left their village. It was only those of us from Mitrovica who were there at the time. On the 6th of May at 8.00 in the morning I went out to bring in some potatoes. We had -- as we had nothing to eat. There was me and eight of my friends, and at that stage I was hit in my spine at 8.00 in the morning on the 6th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks. Can you describe how that happened if you feel like?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, me and my friends, we went two or three houses away from the one we were staying at to try to fetch some potatoes. Potatoes were the only sustenance we had. On our way, we saw the police were stationed in the courtyard of the church. We went to fetch the potatoes, and on our way back my friend says, "My hands or my arms are a bit tired. Can we swap?" At that stage, I had my back towards the police; and all of a sudden I felt some pain in my back and fell down.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, as a consequence of this injury, then you - in paragraph 32 of the statement for reference - you were carried to the village of Zahac. In which municipality is this other village?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: The village of Zahac belongs to the Peje municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I will show you another map, Ms. Sadiku, of the Pec municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I please have on the screen 65 ter number 00032. And if we can zoom on the area just south of Istok, please. A little bit up, please. If you can scroll it up. Thank you. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, can you see the village of Zablace on this map?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could you please draw a circle around it and put a number 1 close to it.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you also see where the village of Zahac is located, the village where you were brought to after your injury?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: The village of Zahac.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you see it on the map or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this exhibit as marked by the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00506, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, in paragraph 34, yes, 34 of your statement, you mentioned that the police expelled the people also from Zahac and that you had -- you were placed on a tractor and you had to join a convoy heading towards Peje. Can I ask you, what did you observe once in Peje?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Police again stopped us when we arrived in Peje and stripped us of all the documents we had on us. I'm talking about travel documents. They tore them apart and burned them down.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 36 you said that the convoy proceeded towards the Albanian border. Do you remember the way you took, the towns and villages you passed by before arriving to the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you -- can you tell us, please, or can you name those villages, or just the road you took towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Peje, Prizren, Zhur, and after that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. And in paragraph 36 again you say that the convoy was stopped in a number of check-points. Can you tell us who manned those check points and what happened at those check-points?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: As I said earlier, police stopped us in Peje. They requested our documents, which they set fire to, and again before crossing the border into Albania, police again stopped us. They wanted money, jewellery. Some people were mistreated and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Did you see -- can did you see check-points also after Peje along the road towards Albania?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes. As I said earlier, before crossing the border area, Serbian police stopped us there.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: What happened there?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: They stopped us, and they asked us to give them 500 Deutschmarks. They said if we did not produce the 500 marks we were to be turned back and not allowed across the border.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, in paragraph 36 you mention that the road you took towards Albania was via Decane, Djakovica, Prizren, and Zhur. Does that refresh your memory? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, what happened when you arrived in Albania? And this is almost the end of my examination.

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: When we crossed the border into Albania, my sister Lutfije [as interpreted], who was with me all the time, she saw one of the customs officers of Albania and told him that I was wounded on that tractor. Later, KFOR forces of the Italian contingent were able to evacuate me and give me the first aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ms. Sadiku, which is your current health situation, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: SADIJE SADIKU
utterances.text: Yes. In the year 2006, I came to testify here before this Tribunal, and I had ten operations on me in 2006. I had an additional two in the meantime. Say for the past ten years I have undergone 12 operations altogether, and I'm in an awful medical situation, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for having -- having answered my question, Ms. Sadiku.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have other questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. D'Ascoli. Mr. Djurdjic, we're very concerned about the length of time that it will be necessary for the witness to remain in The Hague. Can you indicate how long you expect to be in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try to finish both witnesses on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could I please suggest something? As Mr. Aleksandric, as you're aware, needs to leave and to finish his whole entire testimony on Monday. Could we maybe start in chief with him and actually complete the direct examination and cross-examination, and after we finish with him we may continue with Ms. Sadiku if -- if the Defence agrees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will be, we believe, necessary to complete both witnesses by the end of Monday because of their personal situations, and that will require a great deal of time discipline. There are clearly some issues which are worthy of exploration, but there are others that may not be so important and should be left aside. The order in which the witnesses are called on Monday is a matter that is not of great importance to the Chamber, but it may be that it will be beneficial to finish this witness as quickly as possible and then go to the other witness on the basis that we will finish both of them on Monday, and therefore the time spent on each will have to be very limited. It may be discussed between counsel, the order that would be preferred for Monday. We will accept whatever counsel agrees. If there can be no agreement, we would propose to continue first with this witness and then to go to the witness Aleksandric, and we will be watching time very shortly. It will not be possible to spend a full session with this witness if we are to deal with Aleksandric, unless you are able to revise your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that is the course we will take. Please be aware that there are some limited movement problems on Monday because of the international meeting on Tuesday. And movement into and out of this building on Monday will be limited. So if you can make -- take care to ensure, and Victims and Witnesses Unit will be doing it as well, that the witnesses are able to enter the building for Monday. Is there any further guidance that counsel need?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I say the Defence will complete the cross-examination of both these witnesses by the end of Monday. You need not be concerned about that. The timetable, the schedule, may be whatever you decide or whatever suits the Prosecution. The Defence will fit into that, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sadiku, you will be aware that we have to adjourn now for the day because of other commitments. Your evidence will continue on Monday. I'm sorry that it means that you will need to stay here over the weekend. I understand arrangements are in place to ensure that you're as comfortable as can be in the circumstances, and we hope that this will not be too great an inconvenience to you. The people who are assisting you will give you further guidance about your movements on Monday to be here, and we will complete your evidence on Monday so that you'll be free then to leave. Thank you very much. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 30th day of March, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
